about.title: Ross Medical Malpractice Claims
about.longDescription: Ross is a small, tightly-knit Marin County community, but that doesn't mean residents are immune to the harm that can come from a missed diagnosis, a surgical mistake, or a medication error. Because Ross itself has limited medical infrastructure, many residents receive care at hospitals and clinics elsewhere in Marin County, which can add another layer of complexity if something goes wrong. California's MICRA law puts firm deadlines and specific requirements on these cases, including a 90-day pre-suit notice and a near-universal requirement for a qualified medical expert to weigh in. A bad outcome by itself doesn't prove malpractice happened — the law requires showing that a provider's care fell below an accepted standard. If you or someone you love was harmed by a healthcare provider in connection with care received while living in or visiting Ross, our team can help you understand your rights, free of charge.

whyChoose.title: Why Understanding MICRA Matters in Ross

items.title: Strict, Short Deadlines
items.desc: California generally gives you one year from discovering the injury, and no more than three years from when it occurred, to bring a claim. Missing this window can end a case regardless of its merits.

items.title: 90-Day Notice Requirement
items.desc: Before filing suit, California law requires giving the healthcare provider 90 days' advance notice. Our team can help make sure this step is handled correctly and on time.

items.title: Expert Review Is Usually Required
items.desc: Because a bad medical outcome alone isn't enough to prove malpractice, a qualified medical expert almost always needs to weigh in on whether the standard of care was met.

items.question: How long do I have to bring a medical malpractice claim in California?
items.answer: Generally, you have one year from when you discover (or reasonably should have discovered) the injury, but no more than three years from the date it happened. These deadlines are strict, so it's worth speaking with us as soon as you suspect something went wrong.

items.question: Is there a limit on what I can recover for pain and suffering?
items.answer: Yes, California's MICRA law places a cap on non-economic damages, though that cap rises each year under current law. Economic damages, like medical bills and lost income, are generally not subject to this cap.

items.question: I live in Ross but was treated at a hospital outside the city — does that matter?
items.answer: Not necessarily. What matters most is where the care was provided and which provider is responsible, not where you live. Our team can help figure out the right venue and provider details for your specific situation.

items.question: Does a poor medical result automatically mean malpractice occurred?
items.answer: No. California law requires showing that a healthcare provider's care fell below an accepted medical standard, not just that the outcome was disappointing or unexpected. This is why a qualified medical expert is almost always needed to evaluate the case.
